sentences.t: Hola, hola, today we're doing ten Spanish phrases your textbook taught you, and nobody actually says.
Not because the textbook is wrong, exactly, it's just a bit, how do I say this, stuck in nineteen eighty.
Number one, me llamo, my name is.
It's correct, it's fine, but in casual conversation people very often just say soy and then their name.
Soy Lucía, that's it, short and friendly, like you're actually at a party and not at a job interview.
Number two, cómo estás, which every textbook teaches you on page one.
Again, totally correct, but in Spain you'll hear qué tal all the time, and in Mexico, qué onda.
If you say qué onda in Madrid, though, people will know immediately that you learned from Mexican TV, which is cute.
Number three, the famous vosotros.
If you learned Spanish in Spain, you use it every day, if you're going anywhere in Latin America, you will basically never hear it.
There it's always ustedes, for everyone, friends, family, your boss, the dog.
Number four, tengo hambre, I'm hungry, and this one's fine, but people stretch it, like tengo un hambre que me muero.
I'm so hungry I'm dying, that's how my mother announced dinner every night of my life.
Number five, de nada, you're welcome, and in Mexico you'll often hear con gusto or a la orden instead.
Number six, the textbook says el coche for car, but in Mexico it's el carro, and in Argentina it's el auto.
Same thing, three countries, three words, and every single one of them thinks theirs is the normal one.
Number seven, qué hora es, and honestly that one is fine everywhere, I just wanted to give you one easy win.
Number eight, estoy embarazada, which is the classic mistake, it does not mean embarrassed, it means pregnant.
I have watched a grown man tell a room full of my aunts that he was pregnant, and they will never let him forget it.
Number nine, vale, which is everywhere in Spain, it's okay, sure, deal, all of it.
And number ten, the textbook teaches you hasta luego, but in real life everyone just says chao, or nos vemos.
So, a lot of you have asked how to actually get used to the real version of Spanish, the stuff people say in the street.
That's exactly why I made my own course, it's called Habla Real, and it's eight weeks of real conversations.
My friends in Madrid, Mexico City and Buenos Aires just talking normally, and then I break down every phrase with you.
Every lesson comes with a transcript and a little practice section, and you can go at your own pace.
It's on my website, hablareal dot com, and it's the main way I support this channel, so if you join, thank you so much.
Okay, homework for you, write in the comments one phrase your textbook taught you that turned out to be weird.
I'll pick my favorites for a part two, because I know there are a hundred more.
Gracias por ver, nos vemos, chao.
